clinicalPearls: Cocaine blocks reuptake at the dopamine transporter, raising synaptic dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin in both CNS and PNS; this monoaminergic excess underlies its euphoric and sympathomimetic effects.

Smoked or vaporized cocaine (freebase/crack) reaches the brain almost as fast as the IV route because of the large pulmonary vasculature, producing a rapid, intense, transient high that increases addictive potential.

Acute psychostimulant intoxication produces a uniform syndrome regardless of agent: euphoria, increased energy, reduced need for sleep, decreased appetite, heightened alertness, increased libido, plus peripheral tremor, diaphoresis, hypertonia, tachypnea, hyperreflexia, and hyperthermia.

Many psychostimulant effects are biphasic: low doses improve psychomotor performance and increase vagal tone (lowering heart rate), whereas high doses cause tremor/convulsions and raise heart rate and blood pressure.
Combining cocaine with alcohol generates the metabolite cocaethylene, whose cardiovascular toxicity is additive to cocaine's, intensifying pathophysiologic harm.

Methamphetamine is more potent than amphetamine, producing higher synaptic dopamine and greater nerve-terminal toxicity; the dextrorotatory (d-) enantiomer has 3-5 times the CNS activity of the l-form, and smoked bioavailability (~90%) far exceeds oral (~67%).

MDMA acts mainly on serotonin transporters, increasing release of serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine; animal data show moderate-to-high doses can cause loss of serotonergic nerve endings and permanent damage.

Classic (serotonergic) hallucinogens such as LSD, psilocybin, mescaline/peyote, DMT, and ayahuasca disrupt serotonin and glutamate signaling; oral onset is ~20-90 min with duration up to 6-12 h (salvia ~30 min).

Dissociative agents (PCP, ketamine, high-dose dextromethorphan, salvia) distort perception of time, motion, color, sound, and self and can cause respiratory depression, heart-rate abnormalities, and a withdrawal syndrome with craving, confusion, headache, and sweating.

Psychostimulant withdrawal features hypersomnia, increased appetite, and depressed mood; acute withdrawal lasts ~7-10 days but residual symptoms may persist for months. Conditioned (cue-triggered) craving, not physical withdrawal, is considered the primary driver of ongoing use.

Stimulant use disorder is diagnosed by DSM-5 when at least 2 of 11 criteria occur within 12 months; for hallucinogen use disorder only the first 10 criteria apply because the withdrawal criterion does not apply (use is typically not chronic).

Adulterants are a major and underappreciated hazard: cocaine/methamphetamine are increasingly cut with fentanyl-related opioids (overdose deaths), levamisole (agranulocytosis, leukoencephalopathy, cutaneous vasculitis with skin necrosis), clenbuterol (tachycardia, hyperglycemia, hypokalemia), and xylazine (sedation, necrotic soft-tissue lesions).
harrison.pathophysiology: Psychostimulants increase synaptic monoamines. Cocaine binds the dopamine transporter and blocks reuptake of dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin, raising their levels centrally and peripherally; repeated exposure induces long-term neuronal changes including adaptations in glutamate-releasing neurons. Methamphetamine, a cationic lipophilic molecule structurally similar to monoamine transporters, reverses transporter function to dump newly synthesized catecholamines from storage vesicles into the synapse and also inhibits monoamine oxidase, attenuating monoamine metabolism; it is more potent than amphetamine with greater nerve-terminal toxicity. MDMA acts predominantly on serotonin transporters to release serotonin (and norepinephrine/dopamine) and can damage serotonergic nerve endings. Cathinone (from khat) increases dopamine release and reduces its reuptake. Classic hallucinogens disrupt serotonin (affecting mood, perception, sleep, appetite, temperature, sexual behavior, muscle control) and glutamate (affecting pain perception, environmental responses, emotion, learning/memory). The sympathomimetic surge drives the cardiovascular, neurologic, pulmonary, renal, and hyperthermic complications.
additionalDifferentials: Sympathomimetic toxidrome from other agents (e.g., synthetic cathinones/bath salts, prescription stimulant misuse)
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome / malignant hyperthermia (hyperthermia, rigidity)
infectionMimics: CNS infection (meningitis/encephalitis) presenting with agitation, fever, altered mental status
nonInfectiousMimics: Hypoglycemia or hypoxemia (must be excluded before treating agitation)

Chest radiograph in cocaine-associated chest pain
Cardiac biomarkers to exclude myocardial infarction
Note that emerging substances/NPS are often NOT detected on standard ED drug screens or postmortem toxicology
redFlags: Severe psychomotor agitation, hypertension, tachycardia, headache, and mydriasis indicating sympathetic overactivity / overdose
Hyperthermia (goal to cool to core temperature <39 C within 30 min)
Seizures, coma, or focal neurologic signs
Chest pain, cardiac ischemia/arrhythmia, left ventricular dysfunction, aortic dissection/rupture
Respiratory failure, airway burns or bronchospasm from inhaled crack ('crack lung')
Rhabdomyolysis with metabolic acidosis / renal infarction
Concurrent opioid co-ingestion (e.g., fentanyl-adulterated cocaine) precipitating fatal overdose
'Bad trip' with panic, paranoia, or psychosis (hallucinogens), which may persist up to 24 h
harrison.prognosis: Acute overdose is a medical emergency that can be fatal through cerebral hemorrhage/infarction, cardiac arrhythmia or ischemia, respiratory failure, hyperthermia, or rhabdomyolysis, and management is largely supportive in an ICU/telemetry setting. Co-ingestion of other drugs (especially opioids) markedly increases morbidity and mortality, and overdose deaths involving cocaine and psychostimulants have risen sharply (cocaine-related overdose deaths more than quintupled from 2011 to 2022; psychostimulant-involved deaths reached ~36,000 in 2023). Early abstinence is frequently complicated by depression, guilt, insomnia, and anorexia that can be as severe as a major affective disorder and may persist for months to years. Contingency management has robust evidence of efficacy for stimulant use disorder with benefit lasting up to 2 years after treatment ends; no FDA-approved pharmacotherapy exists for stimulant or hallucinogen addiction. Chronic hallucinogen/dissociative use can leave persistent psychosis, memory loss, anxiety, depression, suicidal ideation, and flashbacks lasting a year or more.
pitfalls: Beta blockers should generally be avoided in cocaine users because unopposed alpha-adrenergic stimulation from beta blockade may cause coronary vasoconstriction, ischemia, and infarction; if essential, mixed alpha/beta agents (e.g., labetalol, carvedilol) are preferred over nonselective beta blockers.
Succinylcholine is relatively contraindicated for rapid-sequence intubation in cocaine use; a nondepolarizing agent (e.g., rocuronium) is the alternative.
Before treating psychomotor agitation, hypoglycemia and hypoxemia must be ruled out first.
Drugs sold as 'Molly'/MDMA frequently contain methylone, ethylone, or other synthetic cathinones rather than MDMA, so the reported drug may not match the actual exposure.
Emerging/new psychoactive substances are often missed on standard drug tests, so a negative screen does not exclude intoxication.
Fentanyl, xylazine, levamisole, and other adulterants can produce effects (and overdose) not anticipated from the intended drug.
MDMA, LSD, and psilocybin remain Schedule I in the United States despite FDA breakthrough-therapy designations; investigational use does not equal approved therapy.
harrison.severityClassification: No single graded severity scale; DSM-5 stimulant use disorder severity is rated mild (2-3 criteria), moderate (4-5), or severe (>=6) of 11 criteria over 12 months. Acute clinical severity ranges from intoxication to life-threatening overdose marked by sympathetic overactivity (agitation, hypertension, tachycardia), hyperthermia, seizures, intracranial or cardiac events, respiratory failure, and rhabdomyolysis. Complications of psychostimulant use are catalogued in Table 468-1 across cardiovascular, CNS/PNS, pulmonary, gastrointestinal, renal, endocrine, and other organ systems.
management: First-line control of agitation, hypertension, tachycardia and seizures with intravenous benzodiazepines to dampen central sympathetic overactivity
Aggressive external and internal cooling with sedation for hyperthermia, and intravenous fluids to prevent rhabdomyolysis-related acute kidney injury
For cocaine-associated chest pain, treat with benzodiazepines, nitrates and aspirin, and avoid non-selective beta-blockers because of unopposed alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction
Supportive intensive-care or telemetry management of arrhythmia, ischaemia and hypertensive emergency, using sodium bicarbonate for wide-complex dysrhythmia from sodium-channel blockade
Monitor ECG, core temperature, creatine kinase and renal function, and screen for co-ingestants, especially opioids
Address the underlying substance use disorder with psychosocial interventions such as contingency management and cognitive behavioural therapy, as no agent is licensed for stimulant dependence
Escalate to critical care for refractory hyperthermia, haemodynamic collapse, status epilepticus or intracranial haemorrhage
